title: An Empirical Preregistered Evaluation of Generate–Validate–Repair for Intent-to-Configuration NetOps Tasks
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory experiment that measures operational failure rates when translating high-level NetOps intents into device configurations: (1) LLM-only generation (baseline) versus (2) a guarded generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline. Using a frozen preregistration (GVR-ProtocolEval-2026-PR1), a Dockerized Mininet emulated testbed, and a 200-item stratified intent-to-configuration confirmatory bank, we ran deterministic paired trials with gpt-5-mini. All 200 paired tasks produced valid, verifier-accepted configurations in both arms (baseline = 200/200, GVR = 200/200). The mean paired difference in the operational-failure indicator was 0.00 (95% bootstrap CI [0.00, 0.00]; Wilcoxon p = 1.0). Thus, in this controlled synthetic emulation the preregistered primary hypothesis (that GVR reduces operational failures relative to LLM-only generation) was not supported. We report full preregistered artifacts, deterministic analysis, contamination checks, and discuss threats to validity: constrained scope (emulated devices, public vendor templates), single-model testing, and limited verifier coverage. We close with operational implications: in well-scoped emulated settings, state-of-the-art LLM generation can match guarded pipelines for straightforward intent classes, but guarded architectures retain value for richer environments, broader models, and non-deterministic deployments. All execution artifacts, hashes, and the immutable initial master-prompt reference are disclosed.

sections.introduction: Motivation. Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed to automate NetOps functions such as intent-to-configuration translation, routing changes, and service migrations. Prior literature documents both promising automation prototypes and brittle, safety-critical failure modes (e.g., malformed syntactic translations, unsafe step ordering) that can produce outages. The ideal operational question is whether architectural safeguards (generate–validate–repair, GVR) measurably reduce operational failures when LLMs produce actionable configurations. Our contribution. We preregistered (GVR-ProtocolEval-2026-PR1) a tightly constrained confirmatory study that: (i) defines a paired estimand (per-task binary operational-failure indicator observed under controlled deployment tests), (ii) executes a deterministic 200-task paired experiment in a Dockerized Mininet emulation, and (iii) publishes raw artifacts, deterministic analysis, and the mandatory Disclosure Statement. The experiment tests whether a GVR pipeline reduces operational failures relative to LLM-only generation for a stratified NetOps task bank across protocol families and two interaction modalities (CLI, API).
sections.related_work: Prior work has examined LLMs for network configuration and NetOps benchmarking (e.g., NetConfEval, NetEval, OpsEval) and proposed GVR-style pipelines and verifier-assisted generation as safety mitigations. Representative references from the verified corpus include Changjie Wang et al. (NetConfEval, 2024) and OpsEval (2023), which motivate structured evaluation in NetOps contexts. These works highlight heterogeneity in tasks, verifier models, and testbeds; our study complements them with a preregistered paired design and full artifact publication.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and experimental plan. We froze the design before execution (study_id GVR-ProtocolEval-2026-PR1). The confirmatory bank contains 200 stratified intent-to-configuration tasks (5 protocol groups × 2 modalities × ≈20 tasks per cluster). Tasks are synthetic but vendor-inspired; each task includes initial and expected final states, explicit workflow constraints, and a canonical reference configuration. The estimand is the paired mean difference in a binary operational-failure indicator (1 if reachability loss or policy violation observed during deployment tests; 0 otherwise). Analysis: nonparametric paired bootstrap (10,000 resamples, fixed seed), Wilcoxon signed-rank exact test. Execution harness. Adapter: hosted_netops_gvr_v1; model: gpt-5-mini; execution mode: scientific_confirmatory; planned maximum model calls: 400. Each task was executed once per condition; retries only for infrastructure failures (none occurred). Validator. A deterministic domain-specific validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) deployed configurations into a Mininet-based emulation and checked reachability, dependency rules, and policy constraints. Contamination and integrity. The preregistered contamination detector flagged items with ≥80% token overlap against curated public corpora (none exceeded the threshold). All artifacts, provider traces, and execution hashes were recorded; the initial master-prompt immutable reference is recorded (provenance/master_prompt.txt, SHA-256 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba).
sections.results: Confirmatory outcome. All 200 confirmatory pairs completed without infrastructure failures. Baseline (LLM-only) success: 200/200; Guarded (GVR) success: 200/200. Paired contingency: n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Mean paired difference = 0.00; 95% bootstrap CI = [0.00, 0.00] (bootstrap resamples = 10,000; seed = 1729). Wilcoxon signed-rank p = 1.0. Secondary and exploratory diagnostics. Repair-iteration statistics: no repairs were required (repair_applied = false in all verifier traces for both arms). Automated contamination summary: no tasks excluded. Deterministic reconciliation and accounting checks passed. Representative per-task artifacts, validator traces, and analysis CSVs are published with SHA-256 manifests (see manuscript_evidence_bundle).
sections.discussion: Interpretation. The preregistered primary hypothesis (H1) that GVR reduces operational-failure rates relative to LLM-only generation was not supported in this controlled setting because both arms produced verifier-acceptable configurations for all preregistered tasks. Several plausible, non-mutually-exclusive explanations arise. First, the confirmatory tasks were synthetic, small- to medium-sized, and assembled from public vendor templates; for these narrowly scoped intents a modern LLM (gpt-5-mini) can reliably produce correct sequences that satisfy the validator. Second, the validator's deterministic rule set and the emulation scope (Mininet containers with specified dependency rules) may have favored straightforward correctness checks, reducing the chance for divergence. Third, the chosen model and prompts (shared-initial generation) may have matched training-domain patterns for such vendor-like templates. Operational implications. Results do not imply that GVR is unnecessary in broader settings. We observed no reduction advantage in this emulation for these task families and this model, but GVR architectures remain valuable where (i) tasks are open-ended, (ii) verifiers must reason about richer device semantics or chaotic telemetry, (iii) models are more stochastic, or (iv) production hardware behaviours differ from emulation. The preregistered exploratory aims (iteration counts, failure-class distribution) yielded null repair activity, so failure-mode analysis is limited to the absence of failures.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered paired confirmatory evaluation comparing LLM-only generation and a guarded GVR pipeline on a 200-task NetOps intent-to-configuration bank in a deterministic Mininet emulation with gpt-5-mini. Both conditions produced verifier-accepted configurations in all paired trials; the measured paired difference was zero. The study underscores the importance of preregistered, artifact-backed experiments: null and boundary findings help calibrate expectations about when guarded architectures provide measurable safety benefits. Future work should expand model diversity, broaden protocol complexity, include production device families, and evaluate richer verifiers and adversarial perturbations. All artifacts, analysis code, and hashes are published with the execution manifest to enable independent reanalysis.

limitations: Emulation and synthetic task scope: confirmatory tasks were run in a Dockerized Mininet environment using synthetic, vendor-inspired templates—external validity to production devices and complex topologies is limited.
Single-model evaluation: only gpt-5-mini was tested in the preregistered confirmatory experiment; results do not generalize across models.

Verifier coverage: the deterministic validator used a fixed rule set (deterministic_netops_validator_v5); verifier blind spots (richer device semantics, stateful middleboxes) may change comparative outcomes.
Task selection and difficulty: the confirmatory bank targeted operationally meaningful but bounded workflows; more open-ended or adversarial intents may reveal differing GVR value.
Pretraining contamination: automated contamination checks (≥80% token-overlap) flagged no exclusions, but undiscoverable model pretraining overlap with vendor sources cannot be fully ruled out.
